title: We are patchwork
hookLine: we are all patchwork, and each piece plays its own game (Essays 2.1)

cards: Calm in the meeting, furious in the parking lot. Patient with a stranger's toddler, short with your own mother. Generous on Monday, petty by Thursday.
So which one is the real you? Montaigne takes up that question in the essay that opens the second book of the Essays, and his answer is uncomfortable and oddly freeing. It's all of them.
And none of them stays in charge for long.

teach.b: First, the puzzle. In Of the Inconstancy of Our Actions, Montaigne says that people who study human behavior find nothing harder than fitting our actions together into one steady picture.
We contradict ourselves so often that it's easier to believe we're changeable than consistent. So, he says, it's unfair to judge a person by a single act. Second, the image.

teach.h: EACH PIECE PLAYS ITS OWN GAME.
teach.b: We are all patchwork, he writes, so shapeless and mixed in our making that each piece, each moment, plays its own game.
Then the line that stings: there's as much difference between us and ourselves as between us and other people. Third, the confession. He doesn't exempt himself.
He turns his soul one way and shows one face, he says, then turns it and shows another.
He finds in himself bashful and bold, talkative and silent, truthful and lying, generous and stingy, depending on which side he looks from.
Fourth, the week's patches. Imagination, which can make us ill or well. Custom, which makes anything seem normal.
A head well made, not full. Who are the barbarians? The back shop.
Laugh, don't weep. Montaigne never sews these into one system, and he doesn't try. Each essay is a patch.
This one is a mercy, in two directions: toward the person who snapped at you, and toward the you who snapped back.

how: Readers of Montaigne often take this essay as a reason to go slow in judging anyone, themselves included, by a single act.

o: stitched together from the habits of our parents
a quilt of family stories handed down through the years
made of mixed pieces, each moment playing its own game

games.q: this week in Montaigne: tap the pairs.
p: imagination can make us ill or well
each piece plays its own game

s: Montaigne says a person's character is steady and easy to read
he says nothing is harder than fitting our actions into one consistent picture.
he says there's as much difference between us and ourselves as between us and others
that's his line in Of the Inconstancy of Our Actions.
Montaigne leaves himself out of the patchwork
he lists opposites he finds in himself: bashful and bold, talkative and silent, generous and stingy.

games.q: a friend who is usually kind snapped at someone yesterday. someone asks you: so what is she really like? what would Montaigne say?
o: she's unkind; the snap showed her true self.
she's kind; the snap doesn't count.
don't judge her by one act; we're all patchwork.
games.why: Montaigne says it's unfair to judge a person by a single action, because each piece of us, each moment, plays its own game.

practice: Bring back one recent moment when you were at your best, steady, kind and clear, and another when you were somebody else, rushed, sharp, small. Don't choose which one is real; set them side by side like two squares of cloth.
Both are yours, so breathe with both of them there.

wordCard.voice: We are patchwork. Montaigne's picture of a person: made of pieces, each moment playing its own game, as different from ourselves as from others. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: patchwork. Nobody is only their worst piece, or only their best. I'll be here tomorrow.
